opus-5.5.text:
Thanks, it's great to be here.

I tend to think of our work in a few overlapping buckets, and the distinctions are less about org charts and more about what kind of problem we're trying to solve.

The first is what I'd call **frontier safety proper**: understanding what dangerous capabilities might emerge in our models and building the processes to catch them before they matter. That's the Frontier Safety Framework work. We identify critical capability levels in domains like cyber, bio, autonomy, and machine learning R&D, design evaluations that tell us when a model is approaching those thresholds, and specify the mitigations, both security and deployment, that should kick in when it does. The core idea is an early-warning system: you don't want to discover a capability after it's already deployed and widely accessible.

The second bucket is **governance in the more traditional sense**: how a lab like ours should relate to governments, to other developers, and to the broader international system. That includes engaging with AI safety institutes, contributing to standards, thinking about what good regulation would look like, and asking which commitments are worth making unilaterally versus which only make sense if others make them too. A lot of the hardest problems here are coordination problems. No single actor can solve them, so the question is how to build institutions and norms that make the responsible path the easy path.

The third is more **foresight and strategy**: stepping back and asking what the world looks like as these systems get much more capable. What are the structural risks, not just a model doing something bad, but things like concentration of power, erosion of epistemic security, or competitive dynamics that push everyone to cut corners? This work is more speculative, but I think it's essential, because a lot of what will matter most isn't visible yet in today's evals.

The connective tissue is that we're trying to be decision-relevant. It's easy in this field to do research that's interesting but doesn't change what anyone does. So we're constantly asking what the actual decision points are, inside the company and in the wider world, and what the people making those decisions need to know to get them right.

r001.rationale: Frontier safety work identifies dangerous capability thresholds and uses evaluations as an early-warning system for models approaching them.

r002.rationale: The response describes governance work on regulation, standards, international institutions, and norms for powerful AI.

r003.rationale: The foresight and strategy work anticipates structural risks and considerations that may emerge as AI systems become much more capable.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So I'd say the work on the Frontier Safety and Governance team roughly breaks down into a few buckets, and it helps to think about them in terms of the question each one is trying to answer.

The first bucket is what I'd call frontier safety proper, which is about dangerous capabilities. The question there is: as models get more capable, at what point could they provide meaningful uplift for something really harmful? Think cyber offense, biological and chemical weapons, or a model becoming good enough at autonomy, replication, or manipulation that it changes the risk picture. The work is to define those threat models, build evaluations that give you early warning before you hit a critical capability level, and then have a plan for what mitigations you put in place when you get close. That's what our Frontier Safety Framework is for, essentially: the commitment that we'll evaluate for these things and respond when the evidence calls for it.

The second bucket is more institutional, which is the governance side. Even if you have good evaluations, you need to know who looks at the results, who has the authority to say "we don't ship this," and how that decision gets made under commercial pressure. So a lot of the work is about building the internal processes, the review structures, the ways you escalate concerns, so that the safety signal actually connects to decision-making. I think people underestimate how much of safety is really organizational plumbing.

Then there's a third bucket, which is the external and ecosystem side. Frontier AI isn't going to be made safe by one lab acting alone. So we spend a lot of time thinking about how commitments can be shared across labs, how governments can get the information and expertise they need to be credible evaluators, and what kind of standards or norms would make the whole field more robust. That includes things like working with safety institutes, contributing to industry forums, and thinking about what a sensible regulatory regime would look like.

And then I'd add a fourth, more forward-looking bucket, which is the strategy and foresight work. This is where we try to think hard about what the world looks like in a few years if capabilities keep going. What are the scenarios where things go badly, what are the structural pressures, and what could we be doing now that would make those futures more likely to go well? Some of that is quite theoretical, but it informs where we point the other three buckets.

So the way I'd distinguish them: the first is about measuring the models, the second is about how we as an institution respond, the third is about how the broader ecosystem responds, and the fourth is about making sure we're pointing all of that at the right problems. They're all interconnected, but each needs a different kind of expertise and a different kind of thinking.

r001.rationale: It describes identifying when increasingly capable models could provide harmful uplift and building evaluations that give early warning before critical capability levels.

r002.rationale: It covers external work on shared commitments, government expertise, standards, norms, and sensible regulation for the broader AI field.

r003.rationale: It describes forward-looking work on how the world may change as capabilities advance, including future scenarios and pressures that should shape current priorities.

astra-6.text:
I think a useful distinction is between technical safety, governance, and the work that connects the two. Technical safety asks: can we understand these systems, evaluate their capabilities, and make them behave reliably in the ways we intend? Governance asks: how do we ensure that decisions about developing and deploying them are made responsibly? That involves institutions, standards, accountability, and coordination between actors.

The connecting work is crucial. For example, you might develop an evaluation for a dangerous capability. But then you need to ask: what would a particular result imply? Would it trigger additional safeguards, further testing, or a decision not to deploy? That’s where a technical measurement becomes part of a governance process.

There’s also a distinction between preparing for risks we can already specify and building the capacity to respond to surprises. We won’t anticipate everything about powerful AI. So part of the work is developing concrete safeguards, and part is ensuring that we have the expertise, decision processes, and ability to adapt as we learn more.

r001.rationale: The response discusses evaluating capabilities and safeguards, but does not identify forecasting when dangerous AI capabilities will arrive.

r002.rationale: It mentions institutions, standards, accountability, and coordination, but does not characterize governance as advising on societal rules and institutions.

r003.rationale: It describes adapting to surprises as they emerge, rather than anticipating new considerations that may arise on the path to AGI.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish three broad kinds of work. One is technical safety: can we understand these systems, evaluate their capabilities, and make them behave reliably in the ways we intend? That includes questions about alignment, control, and whether our safeguards will continue to work as systems become more capable.

A second is governance within the organisation. How do you turn evidence about a model into a decision about whether to train it further or deploy it? You need clear responsibilities, thresholds for taking precautions, and processes that can actually change what the organisation does.

And then there’s governance beyond the organisation: how governments, other labs, and the broader public can help establish appropriate standards and oversight, including international coordination.

Those aren’t independent buckets. Technical work helps us understand what risks we face and what safeguards are feasible. Governance work helps ensure that knowledge leads to appropriate action. You need both.
